articles.title: Salmonella outbreak: What we know so far
articles.summary: Hundreds have fallen ill with salmonella infections in an outbreak linked to imported eggs.
articles.body:
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has recently declared a national outbreak of salmonella food poisoning after one person died and hundreds more fell ill with the bug.

Although not yet proven, imported eggs or dishes containing them are the leading suspects as to the cause.

Evidence also suggests people caught the bug while eating out, rather than at home - with catering and food services such as restaurants, cafes or take-aways likely to play a part.

But there is still a lot to be discovered.

What do we know and what questions remain?

What is salmonella and how do you catch it?

Salmonella are a family of bacteria that typically live harmlessly in the digestive tract of animals including cattle, pigs and chicken - which is why eggs and poultry are among foods commonly associated with the infection.

eating contaminated food that has not been cooked properly

coming into contact with infected animals

cross contamination after mixing raw and cooked food in the kitchen for example

Signs to watch out for include stomach cramps, diarrhoea, vomiting or fever. These usually develop between 12 and 72 hours after becoming infected.

In most cases people recover without further help but older people, babies and people with weakened immune systems are at greatest risk of severe disease.

Hospital care with fluids and sometimes antibiotics can help in these cases.

Anyone who is concerned should contact their GP or out of hours service in the first instance.

Yes, cooking eggs and other food thoroughly can prevent infection.

Other ways to protect yourself include washing your hands before preparing food, after using the bathroom and after contact with animals.

In the current outbreak most infections do not seem to arise from food that has cooked at home.

The Food Standards Agency has recently issued guidance to catering businesses on the storage and handling of eggs.

The majority of recent cases - 199 of the 207 - have been in England, including 47 in London and 38 in Yorkshire and Humber.

There have been six cases in Scotland, one in Wales and another in Northern Ireland.

While the cases are spread out, scientists used a type of comprehensive genetic fingerprinting called whole-genome sequencing, which revealed the bugs involved are all closely related.

Tests show there are only a handful of differences in their DNA sequences, which indicate the infections are part of the same outbreak, with a common source.

Why are imported eggs considered the most likely source?

Genetic testing of the bacteria suggests there are similarities with a previous outbreak involving imported eggs.

UKHSA experts questioned 114 people involved in the current outbreak and their answers indicate that eggs provide the "strongest signal" or clue.

Some 24 cases had links to five businesses (which have not been named), with 11 people reporting they ate dishes containing eggs.

Investigations suggest these premises may use eggs that are supplied from multiple sources, including imported sources.

In some localities there have been questions over hygiene practices.

"At this time there is no identified link to UK-produced eggs or poultry," the UKHSA says.

Jacquelyn McCormick, head of incidents at the Food Security Agency, says the standard advice remains unchanged - thoroughly cooked eggs that are handled hygienically should not present a food safety risk.

Infants, young children, those who are pregnant and older adults should only eat runny or raw eggs if they have a British Lion mark or are produced under the Laid in Britain egg assurance scheme.

People who are immunocompromised should follow their doctor's advice.

Meanwhile Dr Kathleen O'Reilly at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine recommends checking out food hygiene ratings when deciding on cafes or restaurants.

The vaccination of commercial hens against common salmonella strains, which began in the mid-1990s in the UK, has been a "major public health success" and has "substantially reduced egg-associated salmonella infections," according to Dr Charlotte Hammer at the University of Cambridge.

Another quality control measure is the British Lion Scheme, launched in 1998.

Any suppliers of eggs given the British Lion mark have to stick to a strict code that covers the vaccinating of hens, regular testing and a passport system to make sure hens are traceable.

Paul Wigley, professor in animal microbial ecosystems at the Bristol Veterinary School, says improved surveillance and detection has also helped.

"However, we do still import a large number of eggs and egg product, and salmonella could be contained within these because the countries in which they're produced don't use that same level of control," he added.

Meanwhile, Mark Williams, chairman of the British Egg Industry Council, said food businesses which import eggs should check their supply lines for vaccination information and that all the food safety checks have been done.

Health experts still need to confirm that eggs are the source and the UKHSA is continuing to interview people confirmed to have caught the bug.

Local authorities will be carrying out tests on businesses that are likely to be involved as well as carrying out some opportunistic testing.

Experts will also need to look at the whole supply chain, investigating where the eggs or egg products have been eaten, supplied stored and farmed, for example.

Once they have enough information an important step would be to limit further infections.

The exact source and country of origin will need to be traced.

One challenge is that when a business imports a large number of eggs, they can come from mixed sources.

The UKHSA has alerted other countries about this outbreak so they can check for any genetically similar infections.

And while salmonella infections occur every year in the UK, outbreaks that grow this quickly are relatively unusual, according to Dr Gauri Godbole at the UKHSA, so scientists will want to examine the factors that led to this situation.

articles.title: ‘I can’t do the things my friends do’: Life as a teenage carer
articles.summary: Young carers face huge disadvantages growing up - one teenager explains what life is like.
articles.body:
Ava-Grace Britton is 17 and studying acting at college in north London. She likes going out, seeing her friends and wants to go to university next year.

Unlike most of her peers, however, she also cares for her father, Paul, who has significant mobility and memory issues after suffering a series of strokes eight years ago.

Along with her mother Karen, Ava-Grace monitors Paul's blood glucose levels, gives him medication and helps with dinner and jobs around the house.

"I worry about him all the time," Ava-Grace told the BBC. "Before I go to college I help him and most days I have to return home quickly to look after him."

She is not alone. Officially, census data suggests there are around 130,000 carers under the age of 18 in England and Wales.

But the true figure is thought to be much higher, with many young carers hidden from view. The Carers Trust estimates there could be as many as 1 million carers under 18, with another 500,000 aged 18 to 25.

For some the responsibilities are significant, amounting to more than 50 hours a week - with consequences on young carers' social and academic prospects.

Paul's strokes were brought on by a sepsis infection, which he caught after cutting his thumb at work. His health is further compromised by diabetes which needs careful monitoring.

His condition deteriorated so much he had to give up work as a borehole engineer. He is now cared for full-time by Ava-Grace and Karen, who runs her own charity which organises lunch clubs for the elderly and vulnerable.

"It turned our life upside down," said Karen.

"Paul spent three months in hospital and in rehab. I don't know how I would cope without Ava-Grace."

Ava-Grace says her caring responsibilities have demanded a number of trade-offs over the years.

"You have to make sacrifices. I can't do all the things my friends do," she said.

"At one point I was really enjoying dance and could have started competing, but it would have been a huge time commitment which wasn't possible.

While enjoying college now, she had to move schools several times after being bullied and struggling with attendance because of her caring responsibilities and epilepsy, which she has to manage.

"I worry about the future," she said. "I really want to go to university, but can't imagine going anywhere too far from home. I know my dad needs me."

More than half of young carers, like Ava-Grace, provide support to parents.

The rest mainly look after siblings and grandparents. The Carers Trust says there has been a big rise in non-parent carers in recent years as the cost of living crisis has meant parents have had to prioritise earning money, leaving children to care for other family members.

That can make socialising and pursuing hobbies difficult as well as lead to higher rates of bullying, school absence and even suspensions.

Young carers are 25% less likely to achieve five GCSE passes including English and Maths than their peers, according to Department for Education data.

As a result they are twice as likely to be out of education, employment or training for two years or more.

Some support is available. Young carers are entitled to assessments from their local council to look at the impact on their health, education and wellbeing.

"When young carers get these it can make a real difference," said Andy McGowan, the lead on young carers at the Carers Trust.

"But it takes many years of caring before they are actually identified. And then the support in place to help is patchy, it really depends on where you live."

McGowan, who was a young carer himself to both his parents, says even when help is given to the young in the form of respite breaks, peer support and counselling, the underlying issue – the caring demands being placed on them – is often not addressed.

"The threshold to get adult social care from councils to relieve the caring burden is so high, many don't get help. Until that is addressed, the inequalities young carers face will not be tackled."

The NHS could do more, he added, particularly in terms of preventative and early support for things like substance misuse and mental health, which are also contributory factors to the caring responsibilities young carers have.

"Often young carers are left to fight their own battles for too long - and so school and their own health come second," he said.

In July, the government published an action plan for unpaid carers which included measures to support young carers, including improved help in schools and joined-up support between the NHS, social care and education.

Other parts of the UK have their own policies – in Scotland, for example, there is a dedicated young carers' grant.

"Through our new national care service, this government is determined to build a system that recognises the extraordinary contribution of unpaid carers, supports them better and, in particular, helps young carers," a government spokesman told the BBC.

For families like the Brittons, more help cannot come soon enough.

"I worry about the impact caring has on Ava-Grace," said Karen.

"She has had to grow up very quickly – that has had benefits, she is calmer and more mature than many girls her age and she has a real strength about her. But Ava-Grace and others like her need more help and understanding."

articles.title: Harvest price hike hits business with 1500% increase in bills
articles.summary: Richard Haldenby says his average monthly bill for Harvest had risen from $130 (£95.50) to $2,110.
articles.body:
Customers have shared their outrage after an app used by many businesses to track timesheets and produce invoices hiked bills by as much as 1500%, with one person calling it "daylight robbery".

Richard Haldenby, head of UK consultancy firm Salentis, told the BBC his monthly bill had risen from $130 (£95.50) to $2,110.

Others have reported similar price hikes online, with one person in the US saying their annual charge went from $2,800 to $23,000.

A Harvest spokesperson said customers on "outdated" legacy plans, some dating back to 2011, faced larger price increases as the product became "a significantly more powerful" tool.

They added customers are notified "30 days" by email and then "10 days before their renewal date" and can switch plans "in one click" or request help finding a better price.

Harvest was acquired by the Italian tech company Bending Spoons in 2025, and changed its pricing structure the following year.

Many businesses who pay annually are only now finding out about the increase, as their payment is now coming up for renewal.

Haldenby, whose business consists of up to 15 staff in the UK at any one time, with sister companies also in the US and Australia, said he was "in shock" when he received an email detailing the price changes.

"We have used Harvest in our three companies for at least 15 years and have been loyal and enthusiastic advocates of it," he said.

"But if we were to accept this increase it would double our IT spend for the year, which is completely unaffordable."

Until the change, businesses paid a flat monthly fee for each user.

They could add or remove users as their staffing needs changed, meaning they only paid for the people who needed access.

Under the new usage-based pricing model, businesses can also be charged according to the number of active projects, clients and tasks they have - as well as the amount of revenue they invoice through the platform.

Haldenby said he contacted the company to say his firm would not accept the change.

He was then offered a discount for the next year - taking the price down to $1,309 - which would need to be paid up front.

But he said he believed this would just "delay the inevitable", so he is "planning to migrate to a similar but less good service".

"It's a classic example of corporate greed over valuing customers," he said.

The move has drawn criticism online, with one analyst telling the BBC it was "extremely bad practice".

"Harvest has completely failed at the transparency test," said Mark Peacock, head of the UK consultancy firm PriceMaker, which focuses on pricing strategy for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

"There is no way for a customer to work out how much it's going to cost them until they get their bill at the end of the month.

"Many users are reporting a 10-fold increase in costs which is entirely unacceptable."

Damian Foks, head of consulting at Valueships, said the Harvest price hike was "a clear sign of a shift in the company's strategy from growth to monetization".

He said this was "likely" a result of the firm being taken over by new owners.

Bending Spoons has acquired more than 50 major tech firms since it was founded in 2013, such as Evernote, Vimeo and WeTransfer.

The business has a track record of raising prices in companies it has acquired in the past.

Following its 2022 acquisition of the note-taking app Evernote, the company implemented sharp subscription price increases alongside layoffs in the US and Chile.

Both WeTransfer and Vimeo have faced tighter limits on free tools since they were separately acquired by the Italian tech firm, with legacy users also forced to move onto more expensive pricing tiers.

articles.title: Greenock: The town whose council wants migrants to move in
articles.summary: Greenock wants to attract immigrants to settle in the town and reverse its declining population.
articles.body:
A new shop opened along Greenock's fading High Street in May. Anik African Store has brought a small corner of Nigeria to the Scottish town, selling yams, plantain, okra and catfish.

It is not the only African food shop here - there is another just metres away, responding to the area's changing population.

Five years ago, locals say, it would have been rare to see a black person in Greenock. Now hundreds of Africans and refugees have moved to the area.

The local council has in fact come up with a plan to attract even more to this corner of the west of Scotland as a means of stemming its falling population.

Scottish people "are lovely and accommodating", says Anik's owner, Christianah Omilana, who came to the UK in 2021. "Immigrants will come when there is work", she adds.

The lack of work however has been a key driver of depopulation in Greenock and the wider Inverclyde area. No local authority in Scotland has been hit harder by population decline.

The number of residents in Inverclyde is 22,000 fewer than in 1981. And its current population, 78,000, is projected to fall by a further 16% over the next two decades.

Tackling the lack of people is the council's number one priority, by keeping more residents here and attracting others into the area.

It is a "lovely, friendly" town, says one of Anik's customers, Sunday, who has just moved here from Devon. He has begun a job at a hospital in Glasgow, and has come to Greenock to join his wife who works at the local hospital, Inverclyde Royal.

"If the local council can provide [jobs], everything in Greenock will change, because people [from Africa] would like to come," says Sunday.

Michael Buchanan and Adam Eley visited Greenock for the latest in a series of reports reflecting the range of challenges facing communities across the UK.

Most of Greenock's African population are working or studying in Glasgow or Paisley and have been attracted to the town by cheap housing. Many have arrived on skilled work visas, known as sponsorship, helping to bolster the health and care workforce.

Inverclyde Council's repopulation strategy is based on trying to encourage them to set down roots here, as well as attracting other legal migrants and people who've been granted refugee status to move in.

However, the lack of jobs lies at the root of the town's problems.

"It's a ghost town," says Tiffany, a mother of one, who we met at a local parent and toddler group. "There's just nothing in it. There's nothing to do, there are no shops. There is no employment."

The 29-year-old moved away from Greenock to work but came back to bring up her child. Now, she says she is facing up to leaving once more.

"I'm struggling to find jobs that suit both childcare and myself. I've considered moving from here to Paisley because there is so much more to do there."

Rummage through Greenock's industrial history and you will find a distinct heritage - in the 19th Century its status as a global hub for refining sugar earned it the nickname "Sugaropolis". Thousands of ships were also built in the coastal town over a near 300-year period.

More recently, the computer manufacturer IBM employed more than 5,000 people at its campus near Greenock. But the site closed completely in 2016.

Indeed, in the past four years, a further 1,500 jobs have vanished. Amazon, EE and a string of other companies have gone elsewhere. Just this week , the local shipyard announced it was cutting about a quarter of its workforce. Meanwhile, supporters of Greenock Morton, the local football team, have set up a fighting fund to try to stave off financial collapse at the club.

The town has been left bereft - little wonder Scotland's First Minister John Swinney is due to visit this month, to hear the problems first-hand.

While health and social care roles employ many of the Africans, job opportunities for those born locally, and refugees, can be hard to find.

"When the work disappears, people disappear," says Muriel, one of dozens of elderly residents gathered at Lyle Gateway Community Cafe, a stone's throw from the High Street.

Between games of table tennis and cheap, hearty lunches, the group remembers a vibrant town, full of people and shops they wanted to go to.

There is a despondency now, with words like "depressing" and "empty" peppering the conversation. The pensioners are sceptical too of the council's repopulation strategy. While happy for migrants to move in, they wonder how sustainable any influx would be.

The council requires hundreds more immigrants each year just to keep the population stable.

"Where would they work?" asks Pamela. "The people in Greenock can't get work [never mind] bringing in other people."

The cafe is housed in Lyle Kirk, where Jonathan Fleming has been the Church of Scotland minister for the past five years. He feels the town's depopulation crisis at first-hand. His church does "a lot more funerals than we do weddings and baptisms," he explains. "And that shift, it's a lot more dramatic than it used to be."

The church has been supporting some Iranian refugees recently and their experience is a sobering one, says Fleming. They are desperate for paid work but can't find any.

"They're wanting to contribute to the community. They want to be independent of receiving financial aid and they're not able to do it - they're actually trapped in it, in some respects."

The number of people arriving in Inverclyde from overseas has trebled in recent times, to about 750 per year since 2023. Hundreds of African migrants have now settled in the area, as well as refugees from Ukraine, Afghanistan and several other countries, many with a positive tale to tell.

As part of its repopulation plan, the council is offering English classes for those who need them and help to access skilled employment. Schools are also supported to provide an inclusive "anti-racist education".

Mo Almalarashid arrived in Greenock in 2018 as a Syrian refugee without a word of English. He says he found a supportive community and, after studying hard, he now works as a local gym instructor. "There was always people there for me," he says.

There have been tensions. A local teenager was sentenced to 10 years in prison last year for planning mass murder at the local mosque. And in June, a protest outside a local hotel housing asylum seekers resulted in one woman being charged with a hate crime , and three police officers being injured.

Yet in May's Scottish Parliamentary elections, Reform UK - which campaigns strongly for lowering immigration nationally - came a distant third in Inverclyde, about 8,500 votes behind the winning SNP candidate, and despite fielding its Scottish leader in the constituency.

Other council areas will face Inverclyde's depopulation challenge in the coming years. The populations of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland are all expected to begin declining within the next decade.

Stephen McCabe, who has led Inverclyde's minority Labour-led council almost exclusively since 2007, believes its repopulation plan is beginning to take effect. The population has stabilised in the past two years, he says, largely because of immigration.

Repopulation is at the heart of everything Inverclyde Council hopes to achieve, McCabe says, from housing projects and the revamping of school buildings to, perhaps most importantly, job creation.

'Just push us into the sea': The frustration of an area failed by politics

Why one small town with very little immigration turned to Reform UK

What an empty car park tells us about the UK's debt problem

Standing on the banks of the Clyde, he sees opportunities in the maritime, renewables and defence sectors, reimagining use of the river for the 21st Century - although for that, they will need significant Scottish and UK government support.

When asked about asylum seekers, who for the most part are not permitted to work as they await Home Office decisions, McCabe acknowledges there is "an unease, no doubt about it".

While the council has "willingly" participated in a Home Office dispersal scheme - accepting more than 200 people seeking asylum - he believes the area "has been allocated a disproportionate share", with a Home Office contractor said to have bought up a number of houses in the area.

But migrants and refugees who can work are welcome in Inverclyde, McCabe says.

"Without those people, our health service would really be struggling... The refugees who have come have brought benefits to this area. They will bring ambition. They'll bring children to this area."

Greenock's population is not just shrinking, it is also ageing. The lack of children means that one nursery is closing, while older people have greater health needs.

Add in the area's high levels of deprivation, and there is increasing pressure on public services amid a shrinking tax base. Those who remain, pay more - council tax rose by almost 8% locally this year.

Yet you do not need to look far for a different vision for Greenock. Just 15 minutes down the road is the centre of Gourock, once similarly deprived, which has a small, thriving High Street with independent retailers, boosted by a recent £5m council investment and residents with more spending power.

Local resident Matthew Quinn, a 19-year-old former member of the Scottish Youth Parliament, says Gourock has embraced its future as a commuter town and believes other parts of Inverclyde should follow suit.

The council's focus on creating lots of jobs locally is misplaced, Matthew believes. Many people now work from home, he says, and the area's proximity to Glasgow - about 40 minutes away - should be exploited.

"If we accepted that the jobs are in Glasgow, then our focus should be on public services and ensuring we have a nice environment for people to live. Then I think we would be much more successful," he says.

"It's not that [people] are desperate to leave, it's that there's no reason to stay."

That is a challenge that some Greenock residents are attempting to tackle, head on.

Derek Mitchell, infused with infectious positivity, is looking to convert a former sugar refinery next to an Aldi car park into a thriving hub that will teach and enthuse young people.

A focus on science, technology, engineering, arts and maths, he says, will provide them with skills for the future.

"If you build a sense of belonging, naturally and organically, people don't want to leave."

He has purchased the building as part of a group of locals, who estimate it will need £5m of investment as they continue to look for partnerships.

"A lot of people are starting to do things for themselves," he says. "They see there's potential - they're fed up of waiting."

At a time when much of the UK has concerns about immigration, Inverclyde's decision to embrace migrants and refugees makes it stand out. Its lack of people is acute, its solution, striking. Other communities will soon face a similar depopulation challenge and may look to what Greenock is trying as a possible way ahead.

articles.title: Leaderless Oldham Council faces government takeover
articles.summary: The Greater Manchester authority has been in no overall control since the local elections in May.
articles.body:
Government commissioners could be brought in to run a leaderless council, after councillors once again failed to form an administration.

Members of Oldham Council held an extraordinary meeting on Thursday evening to resolve the stalemate of no political party having an overall majority.

The authority's chief executive is now advising the government of the situation, which came about after Labour lost eight seats and Reform UK took seven in the elections in May, leaving no party with an overall majority.

An Oldham Council spokesperson said: "As a result, the council's monitoring officer will write to the Secretary of State to formally advise of the situation."

The spokesperson said council services continued to operate as normal, and arrangements remained in place to ensure the council could fulfil its statutory responsibilities and continue delivering for residents, communities and partners across the borough.

"We will now await further correspondence from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government," they said.

The latest meeting was called following a report by the council's top legal officer, Alex Bougatef, who said it was his legal duty to declare the local authority is breaking the law.

Presenting the report, Bougatef said the lack of anyone in charge raised serious concerns about decision-making, accountability, and effective governance.

He said: "The appointment of a leader is not optional. It's a statutory requirement."

On Thursday evening, seven proposals were put forward and all of them failed to pass, the Local Democracy Reporting Service said.

Labour and Reform put forward bids to form a minority administration, as well as an alliance made up of smaller parties and an independent councillor.

Reform also put forward proposals that would see councillors elected at the ballot box in May 2027, arguing it should be up to the people to decide.

However, other parties argued this was not a "quick fix" and described the proposal of further elections as "passing the buck", warning the council would still require a leader over the coming nine months before any election.

Bougatef's declaration, which came in what is called a Section 5 report, set in motion a process that could see outside intervention in the wake of no solution.

He has warned there could be 'significant' financial costs coming down the line should commissioners be required.

Commissioners are officials sent by the UK government to help run councils deemed to be failing or breaking the law, most often when a council is declared bankrupt.

Commissioners being imposed due to a political quarrel such as has arisen in Oldham is thought to be a first and could cost £1,200 or more a day.

Conservative councillor Beth Sharp said: "Doing nothing comes at a cost and that cost isn't being paid by us.

"It's paid for by the residents who elected us."

Chief executive Shelley Kipling said, while council services are continuing as they did before, the lack of a leader or elected members in key roles puts at risk how key children's and adults services are assessed

In a plea to members, she said: "I am hopeful we can find a way forward that reflects an immense amount of work that has gone on behind the scenes."

In response to a question later in the meeting, she said the government had escalated their oversight of the situation in recent weeks, telling councillors this suggested an "anticipation of a requirement for government intervention or greater more formalised support".

The government has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Andy Burnham to send high-performing civil servants to mayoral offices
articles.summary: The prime minister said the scheme would help communities "unleash and unlock their potential".
articles.body:
High-performing civil servants will be sent to work in mayoral offices in England, as part of the prime minister's efforts to transfer power from central government to local leaders.

The pilot scheme, due to start in the autumn, will see every mayoral authority get between five and 10 civil servants for a six to nine month period.

The 18 mayors will be able to request civil servants with the particular skills they need and Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the scheme would help communities "unleash and unlock their own potential".

The announcement followed a virtual meeting between local mayors and the prime minister, who was working from his new No 10 North office in Manchester.

A series of devolution deals over the past 10 years have seen mayoral authorities - made up of local councils and elected mayors - given power and funding over areas such as transport and housing.

Mayoral strategic authorities have been established in areas including Greater Manchester, the West Midlands and West Yorkshire but not in others, for example Surrey and Cornwall.

Further measures announced by the government include a new civil service fast stream pilot for local authority roles in Yorkshire and Humber.

The fast stream programme recruits between around 700 and 1,400 people each year, who are then placed across different government departments.

Applications for the new Yorkshire and Humber scheme will open in October with successful candidates starting in September 2027.

The Future Leaders Scheme - which provides training and support for senior civil servants - will be opened up to those working in mayoral and local authorities.

A digital devolution programme will create a data-sharing model between central government and mayoral authorities.

Burnham spent almost a decade as Greater Manchester Mayor and since becoming prime minister has repeatedly said he wants to devolve power away from central government.

During his leadership campaign, he announced he would set up a new Downing Street team based in Manchester, called "No 10 North".

The new unit, overseen by senior minister Louise Haigh, has been tasked with being the "dominant driver of the UK's economy".

Successive governments have said they want to move more civil servants out of London and last year ministers set a target to reduce the numbers of roles in the capital by 12,000.

According to the most recent figures, 19.6% of civil servants are based in London and the number has been gradually decreasing for the past four years.

Liberal Democrat local government spokesperson, Zöe Franklin MP, said: "Andy Burnham is again putting metro mayoral regions first with this staffing trial.

"Local authorities across the board should be given the same funding and staffing opportunities if he truly wants to grow every region in England."

articles.title: Scottish National Investment Bank makes 'painful' £138m net loss
articles.summary: The publicly-owned body, which operates independently, has invested in several firms that collapsed last year.
articles.body:
The Scottish National Investment Bank has revealed it made a net loss of £138m last year.

The state-owned body cited the collapse of three of its early investments - including its first, Glasgow-based laser company M Squared.

However, the bank also generated an income of £32m, comfortably covering its operating costs of £20m.

Chairman Willie Watt called the losses "painful" but said the bank had learned lessons.

The Scottish National Investment Bank, which is independent from government, was set up by ministers in 2020 with a mission to fund business and innovation to boost economic growth.

Its report for the 2025-26 financial year revealed a net loss of £138m, including £65m of realised losses from the failure of three early investments - M Squared Lasers, the electric car charging firm Trojan Energy and the satellite and digital company Krucial.

There was a further £85m of unrealised losses after rocket manufacturer Orbex and medical technology firm Pneumowave entered administration.

The bank also invested a record £374m in Scottish ventures, while its operating costs were below budget.

Watt said: "The realised and unrealised losses we have seen in this financial year reflect that and are not where we want to be.

"While these figures are painful for the bank, they are particularly so for the businesses which failed and of course for their teams."

He cited a tough economic environment with "tighter financial conditions, cautious sentiment and more challenging fundraising".

Watt added: "We have learned a lot over the past five years and continue to improve and tighten our investment processes along with stricter criteria for potential investments as set out in our investment strategy."

Chief executive David Ritchie called the losses "regrettable and disappointing", but said he was determined to demonstrate that a "commercially disciplined development bank can deliver for Scotland".

Which companies backed by the bank have folded?

M Squared Lasers - the Glasgow technology firm was hailed by Nicola Sturgeon as "a great example of the ambitious and innovative companies we have here in Scotland" when the national investment bank was launched in 2020. It went into administration in 2025 with debts of £64m

Trojan Energy - the Aberdeen-based electric vehicle charging firm collapsed into administration with debt of almost £30m last year

Krucial - the Glasgow-based start-up, which specialised in satellite technology, folded last year.

Orbex - set up to run a planned satellite launch facility in the north-west Highlands, the company is to be liquidated and its assets sold off

Pneumowave - headquartered in Glasgow, the medical tech firm appointed liquidators in July

Since being set up in 2020, the bank has investment more than £1.2bn in 53 ventures and helped to raise £1.9bn in third-party investment.

An independent report by Sir John Elvidge , a former chief civil servant to the Scottish government, found that the bank was expected to have made losses of about £110m by the end of 2025-26 financial year.

He said it was important that the bank learned lessons from the losses, but did not say the scale of the failed investments were necessarily higher than should be expected for a newly launched body.

Responding to the bank's annual report, First Minister John Swinney said it must be able to take risks to deliver "greater economic returns".

He said that principle was essential to "constructing an economy that is fit for the 21st Century".

Scottish Labour economy spokesperson Daniel Johnson said: "These losses must be examined and the bank's leadership must continue to work to identify investment opportunities that will deliver for our economy and our communities."

Kim Schmulian, Reform UK Scotland's finance spokesperson, said: "This is yet another example of SNP ministers gambling with taxpayers' money while those responsible try to dress up failure as a 'challenging environment'."

Scottish Conservative finance spokesman Craig Hoy said that the bank "must not become another SNP vanity project where taxpayers are left to foot the bill for failure while ministers dodge responsibility".

articles.title: HPV home-testing kits now available for women who have missed cervical screening
articles.summary: Nearly four million women in England can order a self-testing kits to check for high-risk HPV.
articles.body:
Women who have missed a cervical screening appointment in England are to be offered HPV self-testing kits by the NHS.

Over the next year, nearly four million will receive invites on the NHS App or via text message, email or letter to order a free kit to use at home.

Figures show around a third of women who are eligible cervical cancer screening have not taken up the offer recently.

The self-testing kits are designed to get more women checked for high-risk HPV virus, which causes nearly all cases of cervical cancer.

Gem Sofianos-Boorman, 39, said her experience shows how important the screening is.

She was diagnosed with cervical cancer at 28, following screening, and says it was the last thing she expected, given she was young, healthy and had no symptoms.

She had surgery to remove the cancerous cells plus lymph nodes from her abdomen and pelvis to stop it spreading.

"Looking back, I truly believe that going to my screening appointment saved my life. My cancer was found early, which allowed me to have treatment before it spread.

"That's why it's great news that the NHS is making it more accessible for some people to take part in screening."

Cervical cancer often doesn't cause any symptoms until the disease is more advanced and harder to treat.

"If you receive an invite to cervical screening, or an offer of a self-testing kit, please don't ignore it - it could save your life."

Dr Sue Mann, national clinical director for women's health, said: "Offering millions of women an alternative test they can do from the comfort of their own homes will be a game-changer – making it easier than ever for them to get tested.

"There are lots of reasons that may stop women from getting their cervical screening – embarrassment, lack of time or worries about discomfort – and these kits provide a discreet and convenient option we hope will encourage more women to take up the life-saving test."

Health Secretary Yvette Cooper added: "Cervical cancer is preventable - but that's why we want to make it as easy and convenient as possible for women to keep up with their screening."

The kits contain a swab, similar to a long cotton, bud which is used to collect a sample from the vagina.

It is then sent back to the NHS and if high-risk HPV is found, individuals will be invited to book a follow-up cervical screening appointment.

High-risk HPV increases the risk of cervical cancer, but it does not mean a woman will automatically develop it.

Trials of the self-testing in London suggest it could lead to one in 10 women to come forward for screening – boosting uptake by around 400,000 a year.

Other parts of the UK are also looking at introducing self-testing.

Women aged 24 to 64 are invited for cervical screening every five years – or more frequently if HPV is detected.

Through a combination of HPV vaccination, which is offered to teenagers, and improved screening, the NHS is hoping to eliminate cervical cancer by 2040.

The NHS says cervical screening appointments with a clinician is still the best way to prevent cancer – and even if you have missed an appointment you can still come forward for one.

articles.title: Jersey earnings rise by 1.2% after inflation
articles.summary: Statistics Jersey says the increase is "slightly lower" than the long-term annual average.
articles.body:
Average earnings in Jersey grew by 1.2% in real terms in the year to June, according to new figures.

Statistics Jersey said in June 2026 earnings per full-time equivalent employee was 4.1% higher than in June 2025.

However, once adjusted for inflation - currently at 2.8% for the island - Statistics Jersey said earnings rose by 1.2%.

The Index of Average Earnings June 2026 report said the overall increase was lower than the preceding five-year annual average of 5.6% per year and "slightly lower" than the long-term annual average of 4.2% per year for 1991 to 2025.

It also highlighted average earnings in real terms increased by 0.9% in the private sector and 2.9% in the public sector over 12 years.

However, it said, over 25 years, average earnings in real terms in the public sector decreased by 3% while they increased by 1.2% in the private sector.

Statistics Jersey said the report was determined from earnings data collected from a large representative survey of employers and all Government of Jersey departments.

Chief statistician at Statistic Jersey, Ian Cope, said over the last 25 years real earnings had been essentially flat, meaning earnings and Retail Price Index (RPI) had increased by the same amounts over that 25-year period.

He said the new figures showed there was a faster increase in earnings than rise in prices.

This was the fourth year in which the survey was compulsory for employers to complete.

Matthew Gill, a statistician for Statistics Jersey, said, when looking back at figures going back to 2001, there had not been much a change in real-term earnings.

He said: "It's not necessarily that people are earning less.

"With inflation going up, it is generally something that people will notice more.

"A lot of the inflation recently has been things like petrol, which people notice when topping up their cars and has an effect on deliveries for food and that type of thing."

Heidi Gibaut, executive director at Law At Work, said a lot of the firm's clients had taken on secondary roles to boost their income.

She said: "When I was younger, I did two roles; but it's not a sustainable way of living.

"It's not how you will get the best out of the colleagues that you currently work with."

Gibaut said she felt it was down to employers to make sure the services and products they offered were being done at the right price to stop inflation from getting worse and "ensure colleagues are paid well".

"But it is a really, really hard balance," she added.

articles.title: Plant makes 5.5m extra litres of drinking water for Jersey
articles.summary: Jersey Water says the desalination plant adds about 5.5 million litres of extra water each day.
articles.body:
A utility firm has begun using its desalination plant to convert seawater into freshwater to top up reservoir levels amid the ongoing drought and high temperatures.

Jersey Water announced plans earlier this month to use the plant in La Rosière, Corbière, which it said was predominately used as a "back up" when it became concerned about reservoir levels.

The island's reservoirs can hold a maximum supply of water to last 120 days but levels have declined over the summer, with temperatures rising as high as 39.3°C (102.7F) , and a drought later confirmed .

Mark Manton, Jersey Water's chief operations officer said the plant added about 5.5 million litres of additional water per day.

The island recorded its wettest month on record in February after consistent rainfall, and its warmest June since records began in 1894 , when temperatures hit a record-breaking 39.3°C (102.7F).

Jersey Water said the plant would contribute the extra water into Val de la Mare reservoir, which was the equivalent to around a quarter of the Island's average daily supply.

It said the facility would run at half capacity, unless conditions in the coming weeks and months "require additional water production".

It said the drought had caused reservoir levels to fall to 64%, which it said was "considerably low for the time of year" and while "there remains enough water to meet current demand, the island will need significant rainfall this autumn and winter to replenish stocks".

Jersey Water said the large fire which broke out near the plant on Monday was a "close call" and, had it been damaged, the island would have lost a vital part of its drought response.

Manton said the plant was a safety net during prolonged dry periods and drought but the island could not "rely on it" for its water supply.

He said it was "really important that islanders reduce how they use water".

"The plant has served Jersey very well, but much of it is more than 40 years old and only meets around half of the island's current daily water needs."

The firm said the plant would continue to be used until it was confident reservoir levels had returned to a "healthy level".

articles.title: Peter Clifford to be sentenced over worker Dale Baker's death
articles.summary: Peter Clifford is due to attend court next month after a worker, 30, died while renovating a house.
articles.body:
A man is due to be sentenced after the death of a construction worker more than five years ago.

Peter Clifford, 63, formerly of Holland Road, Felixstowe, Suffolk, pleaded guilty to gross negligence manslaughter at a hearing in February.

Worker Dale Baker, 30, who was from Felixstowe, sustained serious injuries while carrying out renovations on a house in Woodbridge on 15 December 2020, and died at the scene.

A Newton hearing, which is a mini-trial and heard without a jury, is due to be held on 15 September at Ipswich Crown Court, to establish the facts in the case ahead of sentencing.

A warrant for Clifford's arrest had been issued by the court after he failed to attend a number of hearings.

He was arrested by Police Scotland at an address in Aberdeenshire before being brought back to Suffolk.

Newton hearings are held when the prosecution and defence barristers do not agree on what is a fact in the case.

A judge will make the final decision before considering what sentence to hand down.

articles.title: Cumbria controlled burns warning as fire service calls rise
articles.summary: Cumbria Fire Service asks people to postpone controlled burns as land is "still very dry".
articles.body:
A fire service is urging landowners to hold off having controlled burns after having to put out several that got out of control.

Cumbria Fire and Rescue Service said since Friday, crews extinguished five controlled burns - a technique involving burning old, dry vegetation in the hope of lessening the risk of wildfires.

Station manager Dean Readman said some of his crews were still fighting wildfires in Wales , with others stretched to breaking point this summer as blazes spread across parts of the UK .

The service said while it understood controlled burns were used to manage sites, it asked people to postpone burns until cooler, wetter weather arrives as the ground was "still very dry".

It also urged people to avoid parking on dry grass which exhausts can ignite, dispose of cigarettes carefully and avoid using disposable barbecues and campfires.

On Friday firefighters extinguished a small fire in Lady Hall near Millom.

On Monday crews put out two controlled burns near Lupton Reservoir and near Threlkeld and a small fire in Sewell Road, Carlisle.

On Tuesday Penrith crews attended two controlled burns at Underskiddaw near the A591.

articles.title: Trump officials threaten Kennedy Center demolition if court blocks renovations
articles.summary: The justice department has also asked for Trump's name to be put back on the building after it was removed in June following a court order.
articles.body:
The Trump administration has threatened to demolish the Kennedy Center if planned renovations for the performing arts venue are not allowed to be carried out, court documents show.

Attorneys from the justice department have also asked for President Donald Trump's name to be put back on the building after it was removed in June following a court order.

"An order blocking the Board from appropriately recognising President Trump," the lawyers argued, "will cause donors to flee, financial contributions to dry up, and structural rehabilitation to stop".

The venue has been among the storied sites in Washinton that Trump has sought to renovate since he returned to the White House in 2025.

Trump's lawyers have argued that without the renovations the venue "will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down".

They also called the venue "embarrassing to the Nation's Capital".

After the "decrepit structure" is taken down, justice department attorney Brantley Mayers wrote, a determination of what to build on the site will follow, including the option of a large outdoor amphitheatre overlooking the Potomac River.

The threat to demolish the building comes just weeks after the Kennedy Center board voted to add Trump's name back to the facade of the venue and to proceed with a two-year closure for proposed renovations.

Many of the board members who voted are Trump allies who were appointed by the president.

In late May, a US judge ruled that the president's name had been added to the venue unlawfully, as it cannot be renamed without congressional approval.

The judge ordered that the name be removed, and so it was taken down in June.

The case stemmed from a broader legal dispute over the renaming of the cultural institution, which US law designates as a memorial to President John F Kennedy.

It is the latest in series of projects that Trump has taken on since returning to Washington.

He has been renovating the reflecting pool on the National Mall, he wants to construct a 250-foot victory arch , has demolished the White House East Wing to build a ballroom , and has added his name to institutions such as the Kennedy Center and US Institute of Peace.
